slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Log aggregation collects events from many systems into a central location where they can be searched, correlated, retained, and analyzed.
course.why: Attack evidence is often spread across endpoints, servers, identity systems, firewalls, and cloud services; centralization connects the pieces.
course.example: A SIEM receives authentication logs, firewall events, endpoint alerts, and cloud audit records and correlates them into one incident.
course.exam: Central logs/correlation = aggregation/SIEM. Protect log integrity and synchronize time for reliable investigations.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Alerting tools notify defenders when monitored conditions or detection rules are triggered. Effective alerting requires tuning so important events stand out without overwhelming analysts.
course.why: An alert that nobody trusts or notices does not improve security.
course.example: A SIEM rule alerts only after repeated failed sign-ins from multiple countries within a short period, reducing noise from normal mistakes.
course.exam: Too many benign alerts = false positives/noise; tuning must avoid creating false negatives.

course.learn: Security scanning automatically examines systems, networks, applications, or configurations for known weaknesses and risky conditions.
course.why: Automation provides broad repeatable visibility, but findings still require analysis and validation.
course.example: A weekly vulnerability scanner checks servers for missing patches and exposed services, then compares results with previous scans.
course.exam: Scanning identifies candidates; penetration testing may actively prove exploitability. Credentialed and non-credentialed scans provide different views.

course.learn: Security reporting communicates findings, risk, remediation status, trends, and evidence to the people who need to act. Good reports are accurate, prioritized, and appropriate for the audience.
course.why: Executives, engineers, auditors, and incident responders need different levels of technical detail.
course.example: A vulnerability report includes affected assets, severity, business impact, recommended fix, owner, due date, and validation status.
course.exam: CompTIA may ask what belongs in a report or who should receive it. Match detail and action to the audience.

course.learn: Archiving moves logs or records into longer-term retained storage according to operational, legal, or compliance requirements.
course.why: Historical data can be essential for investigations that begin weeks or months after the original event.
course.example: Detailed logs remain searchable for 90 days, then are moved to protected low-cost storage for one year.
course.exam: Retention/archiving decisions should consider compliance, investigation needs, cost, integrity, and access control.

defs: Security Information and Event Management: centralizes and correlates logs/events for alerting, search, and investigation.
Intrusion Prevention System: detects malicious traffic and can actively block it.

course.learn: Vulnerability response turns findings into risk reduction: patch, reconfigure, isolate, remove, replace, apply compensating controls, or formally accept risk. Validation confirms the chosen fix actually worked.
course.why: A scan finding has no value if it is never remediated or if the remediation is assumed successful without verification.
course.example: A team patches a vulnerable service and then rescans the host to verify the vulnerability is no longer present.
course.exam: After remediation, validate—often by rescanning, testing, or auditing. Do not simply close the ticket because a patch command ran.
